lines: The shop gets told one sentence: about two million orders a day, with some clicks.
One engineer hears a mean rate a laptop could handle. Another hears clicks, a busy peak, and replication, and reaches for a real cluster.
Same sentence, two completely different machines. Which reading is actually right?
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
The laptop estimate did divide correctly by the number of seconds in a day. That part isn't the problem.
Something else is still missing from it, and it's big enough to move the final answer by more than a factor of ten. What is it?
answer: Not a mistake in the division. A gap in what got multiplied in at all.

Orders aren't the only thing happening — each one carries its own clicks. On top of that sits a real peak, well above the daily average, and a replication factor that multiplies storage and network load together.
None of those are rounding errors. Each is its own real multiplication the first estimate simply never performed.

lines: Here's the full chain, built one multiplication at a time rather than guessed at once.
Orders a day. Times how many events each order actually carries. Divide by seconds in a day for the mean rate.
Multiply by the peak ratio for the design rate. Multiply by the size of one event for a daily byte count. Multiply by retention and replication for the storage that actually has to be bought.
Run that identical chain twice: once at the mean rate, once at the design rate.
The gap between the two isn't an academic footnote. It's the literal difference between a system that survives an ordinary busy afternoon and one that quietly falls over.
One more quantity worth naming precisely: how much work is in flight at any single instant.

Take the design rate, multiply it by how long one event actually spends being processed, and what comes out is a real count — not an abstraction. It's buffer memory. It's open connections. It's live consumer slots, all at once.
Take that in-flight count and divide it by what a single consumer, or a single pooled connection, can actually hold.
What comes out the other side is the real number to go provision — not a round number chosen because it felt safe.
Three numbers worth carrying around, each one dated and each one tagged with exactly what it is not.

A single-producer Kafka benchmark from a decade ago, on specific, now-old hardware. Today's object-store request floor, per prefix. And a warehouse scan rate, measured directly, right here, on this very machine, rather than borrowed from anyone else's claim.
Here's that same benchmark number used two different ways.
Claiming a brand-new cluster will hit that decade-old number is a claim this evidence has no right to make.
Saying one partition alone won't bottleneck a design rate that sits far below it is the actual, narrow claim that same number genuinely supports.
One chain carries orders all the way to storage, a single row at a time.
The peak ratio decides what actually gets provisioned, not just what's expected on an average day.
One old, well-proven formula tells you how many consumers, pools or queue slots to actually buy. And three dated numbers, each one honestly labeled, round out the rest.
One more, to use this for real: a second business has roughly the same order volume, but every order now needs three separate approval calls before it ships.
Does that change require inventing a new kind of arithmetic, or does it fit inside the chain already built?
answer: It fits the existing chain exactly.
Three approval calls per order are simply three more events per order — precisely the multiplier this chain already has a slot for.
Nothing about calling something an approval instead of a click changes which arithmetic applies; the chain never cared what an event represented, only how many there are and how large each one is.
